1 The diskproxy manual

diskproxy presents a folder to macOS applications as a virtual disk, an NFS volume or a WebDAV share, without ever writing to the folder. A plugin decides what the application sees: which files are visible, which timestamps they carry, how each file’s bytes are put together, and what happens to metadata the application writes back. Source bytes are read on demand, and disk metadata is built in memory, so nothing is copied and no kernel extension, FUSE driver or Python runtime is needed.

This manual is for people who want to use diskproxy, and for developers who want to adapt it. It covers installation, everyday commands, every configuration key, the three transports, writable views, two complete workflows, writing a plugin, the internal architecture, limits and troubleshooting. The README is the short version; the project story explains how the design came about.

1.1 Where it fits

This book is one of nine on the FirstPair photo tools. Each owns one part, and The FirstPair Photo Stack shows how they fit together.

  • tiffgraph walks a TIFF or DNG file’s structure under a fixed grammar and finds its editable XMP packet.
  • phidentify computes a photo’s identities: SHA-256, DNG raw blocks, image data, Lightroom fingerprint, metadata record and preserved digest.
  • phindex keeps those identities for every file of a volume, and aligns two volumes by content.
  • DNG Compare compares pairs and preserves one side byte for byte as deltas against the other, with a searchable metadata section, through dngc.
  • Semantic Unison synchronizes photo trees, sending metadata edits without resending image bytes, and preserves what a shuttle disk brings into the same archives.
  • packdir keeps directories of small files as SQLite archives that still work like plain files.
  • Tursolite is the SQLite and Turso layer under packdir, DNG Compare and Mechanic.
  • diskproxy serves a folder as a virtual disk, such as previews with camera metadata spliced in, and captures ratings into sidecars.
  • Lightroom Repair repairs Lightroom Classic catalogs, previews and Sync without forging their state.

1.2 What diskproxy is for

diskproxy solves one general problem: an application expects files to look a certain way, and you cannot or should not change the files themselves. Typical reasons are:

  • the files are originals you want to protect, such as a camera card or a photo library;
  • the application identifies files by properties that change for reasons unrelated to their content, such as filesystem timestamps;
  • the useful version of a file is spread across two places, such as a small stand-in in one folder and its preview in another;
  • the application writes metadata you want to keep, but not into the files.

Three plugins ship with diskproxy:

Plugin What it presents Typical use
passthrough The folder as it is A protected, read-only view of any folder
pmp A camera card with stable modification times, optionally hiding photos already ingested Photo Mechanic Plus incremental ingest across timezone changes
previews Stand-in DNGs with a large preview JPEG embedded from another folder, and JPEGs with the camera, lens and XMP metadata of a matching DNG Browsing and rating a photo library whose originals are offline

1.2.1 How it protects the source

Every source file is opened read-only, through a root directory descriptor, one path component at a time, refusing symlinks, . and .., and anything that is not a regular file or directory. Plugins never receive a writable descriptor. The HTTP transports listen only on localhost, behind a fresh random 192-bit token, and reject every request that would change something.

Writable views exist, but they are writable only inside a session: written bytes go to a shadow file or an overlay folder in the session directory, and diskproxy stop deletes them. Only what the plugin deliberately saves, such as the ratings captured by the previews plugin, outlives the session, and it is saved outside the source.

A running view is a snapshot of the folder’s structure with live file bytes behind it. If a source file’s size or modification time changes while it is served, reads of it fail rather than returning a mixture of old and new data. Stop and start again after an intended change.

1.3 New in 1.1

This edition covers diskproxy 0.3.0. Since the first edition, the previews plugin has learned to give preview JPEGs their camera metadata:

  • Metadata splicing. A map entry metadata= names a DNG or an EXIF-only TIFF, and the JPEG is served with its camera, lens, exposure, serial number and GPS EXIF, and its XMP packet, without copying image data.
  • One merged EXIF segment. A JPEG that already has EXIF, such as a Lightroom preview, has it replaced by one rebuilt segment: the JPEG’s own tags describe its pixels and win, the metadata file supplies the camera, and the map’s orientation and capture time win over both. There is one XMP packet: the JPEG’s own, unless the metadata file has one.
  • A metadata store. Instead of one small file per photo, metadata_store names a single SQLite file of them, opened read-only and immutable. Map paths are compared in composed Unicode (NFC).
  • Pixel tags stay the preview’s. Color space, resolution and the other tags that describe pixels never come from a metadata file.
  • Dates exFAT cannot hold no longer stop the disk: they are shown as the nearest time it can hold, with a warning naming the file.

Two libraries built this way are described under Two libraries.

1.4 Installing

diskproxy builds with Rust and Cargo. The launcher uses only tools included with macOS: zsh, hdiutil, diskutil, plutil, mount_nfs, ps and nohup. The server builds on any Unix, but automatic mounting is macOS only.

git clone https://github.com/firstpair/diskproxy.git
cd diskproxy
scripts/install.sh --config configs/passthrough.json

The installer builds a release binary and places the diskproxy launcher, the diskproxy-server binary and the older pmp-card compatibility commands in ~/bin; make sure that folder is on your PATH. It seeds ~/.config/diskproxy/config.json from the chosen example only if no default config exists yet, so reinstalling never overwrites your settings. The examples in configs/ are:

Example Plugin and mode
passthrough.json A plain read-only disk of a folder
pmp.json Camera-card ingest for Photo Mechanic Plus
pmp-filtered.json The same, hiding photos already ingested
previews.json A stand-in tree with embedded previews

To update, pull and run scripts/install.sh again. Stop a running session first, so the new binary is used from the next start.

1.5 Everyday use

Once the default config names a source folder and a plugin, these are the only commands you need:

diskproxy start      # or just: diskproxy
diskproxy status
diskproxy stop

start launches the server in the background, waits for it to scan the folder, mounts the result and prints where:

Ready: /Volumes/DiskProxy
Select this volume in your application (under Disks in PMP).
After use: diskproxy stop

Closing the Terminal window does not stop the view. status prints the server’s process ID and the mounted volume. stop finishes any pending capture, unmounts, then stops the server and deletes the session folder.

Each config file has its own view, so several can run at once, such as a photo library and a camera card. --config FILE selects the view for start, status and stop; without it, start uses the default config, status lists every running view, and stop stops the only one or, when several are running, names them and asks for --config. A second start of the same config is refused while its view runs.

1.5.1 Choosing a source or config for one session

A path after start overrides the configured source. --config selects another config file, before or after start, and --set overrides any single key:

diskproxy start /another/folder
diskproxy --config ~/views/library.json start
diskproxy start --config ~/views/library.json --set label=Library

1.5.2 Scanning large folders

Before it can serve a disk, the server reads the whole tree. For a camera card this takes a moment. For a large library the launcher shows progress on one line, updated in place every two seconds:

Scanning: listing folders: 3120 folders, 905000 files
Scanning: reading files: 523000 of 1256465 (41%)

The server logs a summary when it finishes, for example scanned 1256465 files in 2413 folders in 59 s. The launcher waits up to 15 minutes while the server is alive, and stops at once if the server exits with an error. Short scans print nothing. When output is not a terminal, each update is printed on its own line.

Measured on one library, a tree of 1.26 million files scanned in about a minute; the server then used about 1.2 GB of memory, with a 1.8 GB peak during startup. With camera metadata spliced into its 566,000 JPEGs (see the previews plugin below), the same tree scanned in 110 seconds and used 1.9 GB, with a 2.5 GB peak. A second library of 835,383 preview JPEGs, all but 440 with metadata from a 3.8 GB metadata store, scanned in 111 seconds on a busy machine and then used 1.64 GB. Trees of up to 8 million entries are supported.

1.5.3 When the volume is busy

If an application still has files open, macOS refuses to detach the disk, and stop says so and leaves the server running, so the application can finish. Close the files and run diskproxy stop again. Before detaching, stop checks that the mounted volume is still the one it attached, by its volume UUID, so it never detaches some other disk.

1.5.4 The session folder

Each view’s session lives in ~/Library/Caches/diskproxy/sessions/NAME, where NAME is its config file’s name without .json (set DISKPROXY_STATE_DIR to move the parent folder). It holds the server’s startup JSON and error log, the process ID and start time, the attachment details and, for writable views, the shadow file or overlay and the harvester’s log. A session started by an older launcher in ~/Library/Caches/diskproxy/session is still found, as the default config’s view.

1.6 Configuration

The default config is ~/.config/diskproxy/config.json. A general example:

{
  "source": "/absolute/path/to/folder",
  "plugin": "passthrough",
  "mode": "disk",
  "label": "DiskProxy",
  "port": 0,
  "plugins": {}
}
Key Meaning Default
source Folder to present; a path given to start overrides it none, required
plugin passthrough, pmp or previews passthrough
mode disk, nfs or webdav disk
label Volume name, up to 11 UTF-16 code units plugin’s default
writable Disk mode only: mount through a shadow file and capture writes false
mountpoint NFS mode only: where to mount ~/Volumes/LABEL
port Localhost port; 0 picks a free one 0
plugins.<name> Settings for that plugin {}

Paths in a config file are taken literally: write absolute paths, not ~. Unknown keys are errors, so a misspelling is reported rather than ignored.

Settings are applied in this order, later ones winning: the config file, then --set KEY=VALUE, then explicit flags such as --label. --set parses its value as JSON when it can, otherwise as a string, and reaches into plugin settings with dotted keys:

diskproxy start --set plugins.pmp.hide_ingested=true
diskproxy start --set 'plugins.previews.ratings="/absolute/path/to/ratings"'

The launcher reads mode from the config file to decide how to mount, so put "mode": "nfs" in the file rather than passing it with --set. The launcher refuses --mode, --check and --register; those belong to diskproxy-server.

1.6.1 Checking a config without serving

diskproxy-server --config ~/views/library.json --check

This validates the config and the plugin settings, prepares the plugin, prints its startup information as JSON and exits, without mounting or registering anything.

1.7 Choosing a transport

All three transports serve the same view: the same visible files, timestamps and composed bytes. They differ in what macOS sees.

Disk NFS WebDAV
macOS sees An exFAT disk attached by hdiutil An NFSv3 volume mounted by mount_nfs A WebDAV share
Launcher mounts it Yes Yes No; use diskproxy-server serve
Counts as a disk Yes, e.g. under Disks in Photo Mechanic No No
Writes Optional, through a shadow file Yes, into a session overlay Rejected
Status Ready Experimental Ready

1.7.1 Disk mode

The server generates an exFAT disk image in memory and serves it as one HTTP resource, card.img. macOS attaches it with hdiutil as a raw disk image and reads it with HTTP range requests. The boot region, allocation table and directory entries are generated; file contents are mapped to ranges of the source files and read on demand; unused space reads as zeros. The image never exists as a file.

Timestamps on the disk carry valid UTC offsets, so macOS does not reinterpret them in the current timezone. Names are written in composed Unicode (NFC), the form macOS’s exFAT driver uses for lookups, while source files are still opened by their own spelling.

1.7.2 NFS mode

The server runs an NFSv3 server on localhost and the launcher mounts it with mount_nfs, which needs no administrator rights:

mount_nfs -o vers=3,tcp,port=P,mountport=P,nolocks,soft,intr,timeo=100,retrans=5 \
  127.0.0.1:/ ~/Volumes/LABEL

The server has no lock manager, so nolocks keeps file locking local to the Mac. Every file operation reaches the server by name, which is what makes NFS useful for capturing writes; see Writable views. NFS mode is experimental: see The NFS unmount hang.

1.7.3 WebDAV mode

WebDAV serves the tree as a read-only share. It is useful for tools and applications that work with folders rather than disks:

diskproxy-server serve /path/to/folder --plugin passthrough --mode webdav

The server prints a JSON line with a URL of the form http://127.0.0.1:PORT/TOKEN/; treat the URL as a password. It implements OPTIONS, PROPFIND with depth 0 or 1, GET and HEAD with single byte ranges, and rejects every other method with 403. The transport guide lists the supported properties and limits.

1.8 Writable views

Some applications write metadata into the files they show: Photo Mechanic, for example, writes ratings, color labels and flags into JPEGs and DNGs. A read-only disk makes those writes fail. A writable view lets them succeed without touching the source, and passes each written file to the plugin’s written hook, which decides what to keep. Two ways are available.

Shadow file NFS
Enable with "writable": true (disk mode) "mode": "nfs"
Status Ready Experimental
Mounted at /Volumes/LABEL ~/Volumes/LABEL, or mountpoint
Written bytes go to disk.shadow in the session folder overlay/ in the session folder
The plugin sees a write Within about a minute, and on stop About two seconds after the last write, and on stop

Either way, the application reads its own changes back during the session, and diskproxy stop deletes the written bytes after the final capture.

1.8.1 Shadow-file mode

The disk is attached with hdiutil attach -shadow. macOS then treats it as writable, but every changed block goes to the shadow file, and the served image stays read-only. Because the disk delivers blocks rather than files, diskproxy cannot see writes directly. Instead, a harvester process follows filesystem events on the mounted volume, and every minute passes the changed files to the plugin. It reads each file from the mounted volume, so it sees the application’s version.

diskproxy stop asks the harvester for a final pass and waits up to two minutes for it before detaching. If the harvester is not running, stop first walks the whole volume once for files modified since mounting, so no change is lost. If either step fails, the disk stays mounted and stop points at the harvester log.

The harvester can also be run by hand, for example after a crash left a writable volume mounted:

diskproxy-server harvest --config view.json --volume /Volumes/VIEW \
  --since EPOCH --once

--since walks the volume for files modified at or after that Unix time; --once returns after that walk instead of watching. Without --once it keeps watching, every --interval seconds (default 60), until the --stop-file appears. Hidden housekeeping folders such as .fseventsd are skipped.

1.8.2 NFS mode

The first write to a served file copies its presented bytes into the overlay folder; from then on the client reads and writes that copy. New files, new folders, renames and deletions are recorded in the overlay as well, so an application that saves through a temporary file and a rename works normally. Two seconds after the last write to a file, the file is passed to the plugin. When the server receives SIGTERM, which is how diskproxy stop ends it, it passes everything still pending before exiting.

1.9 Workflow: camera-card ingest with Photo Mechanic Plus

This is the workflow diskproxy was first written for. The PMP guide is the complete reference.

1.9.1 The problem

Photo Mechanic Plus records each ingested file’s path, size and modification time, and its incremental ingest copies only files it has not seen. On the exFAT cards examined, the camera wrote modification times without a valid timezone offset, so macOS interpreted them in whatever timezone the Mac was in when the card was mounted. After travelling, the same photo had a different modification time, Photo Mechanic thought it was new, and it copied the whole card again.

No travel is needed: a daylight-saving change shifts the offset at home. A card whose October photos were ingested in Pacific daylight time (UTC−7) read one hour later in November, in standard time (UTC−8), and Photo Mechanic offered all 904 of its earlier files again. A card that is only ever ingested at one offset is safe without diskproxy; a card that spans a change is not, so registering every card and always ingesting through the view is the simple rule. Mixing raw ingests and ingests through the view of the same card makes Photo Mechanic’s history flip between the two readings, and files are offered again.

1.9.2 The fix

The pmp plugin presents the card as a virtual disk with a fixed timestamp convention. For a new card the convention is UTC; a card with existing history keeps the convention its history was made in, for example Pacific time. The plugin works out the offset the card was mounted in from up to three sampled photos, recorded in a small profile on the card when it is registered. Every file the camera writes under DCIM, videos and thumbnails included, gets the same convention. The photos themselves, and their EXIF capture times, are never changed.

1.9.3 Setting up

scripts/install.sh --config configs/pmp.json

You don’t need to name the card. If the config’s source isn’t mounted, or the config has no source, diskproxy uses the one mounted volume that has a DCIM folder and isn’t a disk image (so a running diskproxy view isn’t picked up as a card). If several cards are mounted, it stops and lists them; pass the one you want to start. A path given on the command line is always used as is.

1.9.4 Registering a new card

Finish any EXIF corrections first, then, with the card mounted in the timezone the Mac is currently set to:

diskproxy-server

With no command, diskproxy-server registers the card: it writes .pmingest.dat if it is absent and the profile .pmp-ingest-proxy.json to the card, and exits. If you run diskproxy start on an unregistered card, it simply prints Run diskproxy-server. If the Mac’s timezone changed while the card stayed mounted, remount it first, or give the offset it was mounted in:

diskproxy-server --source-offset=+09:00

Running the command again on a registered card reuses its profile unchanged. --register deliberately refreshes the samples after reviewed edits.

1.9.5 Ingesting

diskproxy start
# In Photo Mechanic Plus, ingest from the PMP Pacific volume under Disks.
diskproxy stop

Then eject the card. The volume is called PMP Pacific for compatibility, even for UTC cards; the label does not set the convention.

To hide photos already ingested, rather than relying on Photo Mechanic’s incremental history:

diskproxy start --set plugins.pmp.hide_ingested=true

The history is read once at start, so restart the view to hide newly ingested files.

1.10 Workflow: a photo library served from its previews

The previews plugin builds a browsable library out of files that already exist. Its guide is the complete reference; this section walks through a whole setup.

1.10.1 The idea

Suppose your originals are offline, but you have two smaller things for every photo:

  • a stand-in: a small DNG such as a Lightroom Smart Preview, which holds the photo’s metadata and a reduced raw image, but embeds only a tiny thumbnail;
  • a preview JPEG at a useful size, for example from an image browser’s preview cache, under a different name in a different folder.

An application that shows embedded previews, such as Photo Mechanic or Quick Look, shows only the thumbnail in the stand-in. The previews plugin serves each stand-in with its preview JPEG embedded, without writing or copying either file.

1.10.2 Building the stand-in tree

Arrange the stand-ins under the folder layout you want to browse, usually the originals’ layout. On APFS, use clones (cp -c) rather than copies: a clone shares its blocks with the original, so even a million stand-ins cost almost no disk space, and writing to a clone never changes the file it came from.

Then write a map file, one line per file to change, as a path relative to the tree followed by tab-separated fields:

2024/trip/IMG_0001.DNG  preview=a1/IMG_0001.jpg
2024/trip/IMG_0002.JPG  orientation=6   datetime=2024:10:02 04:45:42
2024/trip/IMG_0003.JPG  metadata=0/0A1B/0A1B2C3D.dng
Key For Value
preview DNG, TIFF The preview JPEG, relative to preview_root
preview_size DNG, TIFF Optional: the JPEG’s size in bytes
preview_mtime DNG, TIFF Optional: its modification time, SECONDS.NANOSECONDS
preview_dims DNG, TIFF Optional: its pixel size, WIDTHxHEIGHT
metadata JPEG A DNG whose EXIF and XMP the JPEG is served with, relative to metadata_root
orientation JPEG EXIF orientation, 1 to 8
datetime JPEG Capture time, YYYY:MM:DD HH:MM:SS

With all three optional preview fields, the server builds the disk without opening a million preview JPEGs, which makes startup much faster. They are still checked against the real file on every read.

1.10.3 What gets served

For a DNG or TIFF with preview=, every original byte stays at its original offset. The plugin appends a copy of the first image directory (IFD0) after the original data, adds one entry pointing at a new reduced-resolution image (a SubIFD), and appends the JPEG. Only the 8-byte TIFF header is changed, to point at the copied directory. Applications that show embedded previews then find the large JPEG; raw-capable applications still read the original image data. An existing large preview is kept and stays first.

For a JPEG, metadata= adds the EXIF and XMP of a DNG or TIFF, typically the photo’s Lightroom Smart Preview or an EXIF-only TIFF extracted with ExifTool, so the JPEG shows its camera, lens, exposure, serial number and GPS position. The plugin rebuilds the EXIF in a new segment, leaving out the DNG’s image-structure tags and maker note and adding the JPEG’s own pixel size. It reads the XMP segment’s contents from the DNG in place on every read, so they take no memory. The rebuilt EXIF, about 1.3 KB per JPEG, is kept in memory with the rest of the layout. orientation= and datetime= set Orientation and DateTimeOriginal in that segment, overriding the DNG, so portraits display upright and photos sort by capture time; they also work on their own.

A JPEG that already has EXIF, such as a Lightroom preview with Orientation and color space, has that segment replaced by the rebuilt one. The JPEG’s own tags win over the DNG’s, since they describe the preview’s pixels, and the map’s values win over both. Tags that describe pixels (color space, components, compression, pixel size, gamma) are never taken from the metadata file, even when the JPEG lacks them: a camera original’s sRGB says nothing about a preview rendered in Adobe RGB. Its own XMP is kept unless the DNG has XMP, which then replaces it.

Files not in the map are served unchanged. A mapped file that cannot be composed, because its JPEG is missing or the DNG has an unexpected structure, is served unchanged with a warning in the server log, rather than failing the disk.

1.10.4 The config

{
  "source": "/absolute/path/to/stand-in-tree",
  "plugin": "previews",
  "label": "Library",
  "writable": true,
  "plugins": {
    "previews": {
      "map": "/absolute/path/to/previews.tsv",
      "preview_root": "/absolute/path/to/preview-jpegs",
      "metadata_root": "/absolute/path/to/Catalog Smart Previews.lrdata",
      "ratings": "/absolute/path/to/ratings"
    }
  }
}

metadata_root is needed only when the map has metadata= fields. For a very large library, metadata_store can name one SQLite file holding all the metadata files as blobs in a table stubs(key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, exif BLOB), with metadata= giving the key; see the previews plugin guide. diskproxy reads the store itself, through SQLite bundled into the server, opened read-only and immutable, and refuses a store whose -wal file is not empty. Any SQLite writer can produce it. Tursolite, for example, can write it, optionally under Turso’s concurrent (MVCC) mode, and then seal it to an ordinary rollback-journal file that diskproxy can open. Leave out writable and ratings for a purely read-only library. Start it with diskproxy --config library.json start. Check one file through the mounted volume:

exiftool -b -PreviewImage /Volumes/Library/2024/trip/IMG_0001.DNG | wc -c

The result should be the size of its preview JPEG.

1.10.5 Capturing ratings

With ratings set and a writable view, the plugin reads each written file’s XMP metadata and keeps exactly four properties:

Property Meaning
xmp:Rating Star rating
xmp:Label Color label name
photomechanic:ColorClass Photo Mechanic’s color class
photomechanic:Tagged Photo Mechanic’s tag (flag)

Everything else an application writes is ignored. That is deliberate. Photo Mechanic, for example, sets creation dates from a file’s modification time when a JPEG has none, and copies the stand-in’s metadata into its XMP. Keeping its whole XMP block would carry those invented values back towards your originals.

The metadata is found in a JPEG’s XMP segment, a TIFF or DNG’s XMP tag, or an .xmp/.XMP sidecar. Each photo gets a minimal sidecar in the ratings folder, mirroring the tree:

Written file Sidecar
X.DNG, or its sidecar X.XMP X.xmp
X.JPG X.JPG.xmp, so a JPEG never collides with a DNG of the same name
A stand-in served as X.JPG.dng or X.RW2.dng Under the original’s name: X.JPG.xmp, X.xmp

A sidecar is rewritten only when a value changed. Every change is appended to JOURNAL.jsonl in the ratings folder, one JSON object per line:

{"time_unix":1793718040.97,"written":"2015/February/IMG_4193.dng",
 "sidecar":"2015/February/IMG_4193.xmp",
 "fields":{"xmp:Rating":"2","xmp:Label":"Red","photomechanic:ColorClass":"1","photomechanic:Tagged":"False"},
 "previous":{}}

written is the file the application wrote, sidecar the file updated in the ratings folder, and previous the values before this change. The ratings folder must be outside the served tree; the plugin refuses to start otherwise.

Clearing is captured too. When a file captured before is written without one of these properties, because the application removed it or its whole XMP block, the property is recorded as cleared (Rating 0, an empty Label, ColorClass 0, Tagged False), with the old value as previous.

Captured ratings outlive the session. The next time the disk is built, every served JPEG, DNG or TIFF with a sidecar is served with the sidecar’s values merged into its XMP packet. A DNG gets the merged packet appended after its data, through the same copied IFD0 that adds a preview. Only those four properties are replaced; the rest of the JPEG’s own or its metadata file’s XMP is kept, in one packet. An application that re-reads the file after a restart finds the ratings it wrote rather than losing them. The served modification time stays the source file’s.

These sidecars use the Adobe naming convention, so a DNG’s sidecar can later sit beside its original, where Lightroom or another application can read it. To bring the captured ratings into a Lightroom Classic catalog, follow the recipe in Lightroom Repair.

1.10.6 Two libraries served from previews

Two libraries have been built this way. The numbers are observations of each, not limits.

Smart Previews as stand-ins. On a laptop, a Lightroom Classic library’s Smart Previews were cloned into the originals’ folder layout as DNG stand-ins, and paired with Photo Mechanic’s 1600-pixel preview JPEGs: 671,335 DNGs gained the large preview, and 566,365 of 566,556 JPEGs gained the camera metadata of their Smart Preview, as metadata= files. The 1,256,465-file tree scanned in 110 seconds, about 50 seconds more than without metadata, and the server used 1.9 GB, about 1.3 KB more per mapped JPEG. The view is writable, with ratings captured as sidecars.

Regular previews with a metadata store. On a desktop, a Photo Mechanic catalog was built from APFS clones of Lightroom Classic’s ordinary preview levels, needing only the one drive that holds them. Camera metadata was extracted once, from an existing index of the originals’ metadata, as EXIF-only TIFFs written by ExifTool, and stored in one 3.8 GB metadata store of 834,891 entries. Half of these previews already carried a small Lightroom EXIF segment, merged as described above; most are Adobe RGB without an ICC profile, which is why pixel tags never come from the metadata. The 835,383 files in 6,521 folders scanned in 111 seconds on a busy machine (load average 11 to 15), and the server then used 1.64 GB.

1.11 Writing a plugin

A plugin is a Rust crate that implements the Plugin trait from diskproxy-core and is linked into the application at build time. There is no dynamic loading: adding a plugin means adding a crate and registering it in src/main.rs. The plugin guide gives every step, and the hide example is a complete, compiled reference with a patch that registers it.

1.11.1 The trait

pub trait Plugin: Send + Sync {
    fn identity(&self) -> Option<String> { None }
    fn visible(&self, _parts: &[String], _metadata: &Metadata) -> Result<bool> { Ok(true) }
    fn mtime(&self, _parts: &[String], metadata: &Metadata) -> Result<i64> { Ok(metadata.mtime()) }
    fn compose(&self, _parts: &[String], _file: &File) -> Result<Option<Vec<Piece>>> { Ok(None) }
    fn written(&self, _parts: &[String], _file: &File) -> Result<()> { Ok(()) }
}

Every method has a default, so a plugin overrides only what it needs. parts are the path components relative to the source root.

Hook Return Meaning
identity Stable string or None Seeds the disk’s volume serial; None derives it from the source
visible true or false Shows or hides an entry, on direct opens as well as in listings
mtime Unix seconds The modification time to present; the source keeps its own
compose Pieces or None Presents a file as a sequence of pieces; None serves it unchanged
written () A client wrote this file on a writable view; file holds its new bytes

An error aborts the operation; it is never a request to fall back to the unmodified entry. Keep the hooks deterministic for a session, because the disk is built from one snapshot of the tree. Plugins are shared across threads.

1.11.2 Composing files

pub enum Piece {
    Bytes(Vec<u8>),
    Own { offset: u64, length: u64 },
    Other {
        source: Arc<Source>,
        path: Arc<str>,
        offset: u64,
        length: u64,
        stamp: Option<Stamp>,
    },
}

Bytes are generated by the plugin, Own is a range of the file being presented, and Other is a range of a file under another root. Open that root with Source::new, so it gets the same read-only, no-symlink rules. The core checks every range against the file’s size, records each file’s size and modification time, and refuses reads once either changes. When the plugin already knows another file’s size and modification time, it can pass them as stamp, so the scan doesn’t open that file; the stamp is still checked on every read. Composed files are served identically by all three transports.

1.11.3 Receiving writes

written is called with a read-only handle to the new bytes: from the NFS overlay, or from the mounted volume for a harvested shadow-file view. The source is never written, and the handle cannot write to it. A plugin that saves something should save it outside the source, as the previews plugin’s ratings folder must be, and should treat the call as untrusted input: temporary files, partial saves and files the application writes for its own purposes all arrive here.

1.11.4 Registering and testing

To register a plugin, add its crate to the workspace and the application’s dependencies, add its name to PluginName in src/main.rs, validate its plugins.<name> settings before any setup I/O, and add a construction arm that returns the source, the plugin and its startup information. Test with synthetic folders only, through both direct opens and listings, and confirm that the source files are unchanged afterwards.

A plugin is trusted code. The trait is a policy boundary, not a sandbox: a plugin can call any API Rust allows, so keep its own writes small, explicit and documented.

1.12 How it works

1.12.1 Components

Component Location Responsibility
Core crates/core Read-only source access, the view, the exFAT builder, HTTP, WebDAV, NFS and harvesting; nothing application-specific
PMP plugin plugins/pmp Camera layout, card profiles, timestamp conventions and history filtering
Previews plugin plugins/previews The preview map, DNG and JPEG composition, and ratings capture
Application src/main.rs Config loading, overrides, plugin selection, and the harvest and unmount commands
Launcher bin/diskproxy The background process, mounting, harvesting and the start/status/stop lifecycle

1.12.2 Sources and views

A Source opens its root directory once. Every lookup walks from that descriptor one component at a time with openat and O_NOFOLLOW, rejecting empty components, ., .., embedded slashes and NUL, and returning only read-only regular files and directories. A View combines a source, a plugin and a volume label, and every transport serves through it.

1.12.3 Building the disk

The scan runs in two phases. A serial walk lists every folder and adds a placeholder for each file. Then a parallel phase opens and lays out the files, one directory per task, each file opened relative to its already-open folder, and calls the plugin’s compose for each. A reporter thread prints progress every two seconds on long scans.

The layout keeps each name once, with a link to its parent folder, and rebuilds full paths only when a file is read; each file’s pieces become extents in the disk’s map. After building, the server returns freed startup memory to macOS, so its resident size reflects what it keeps.

A disk read finds the extents covering the requested range: generated metadata, zeros, or ranges of source files. Before reading a source file, it checks that file’s size and modification time against what was recorded at scan time.

1.12.4 The NFS server

The NFS transport is built on the nfsserve crate and runs on tokio. It presents the same view by path. Its overlay keeps client-written files, client-created folders and the paths the client removed or renamed away. Presented metadata is computed on first use. A settle timer passes each written file to the plugin once it has had no writes for two seconds, and a SIGTERM handler flushes the rest.

1.12.5 The launcher

bin/diskproxy starts diskproxy-server serve in the background with its output in the session folder, polls the startup JSON for the disk URL or NFS port, shows scan progress, and mounts. For a writable disk it also starts the harvester and records its arguments, start time and the mount time, so stop can finish or replace it. stop reverses each step and checks identities on the way, so it never detaches a different disk or stops a different process.

1.13 Limits

  • Disk mode: names must be UTF-8 and valid for exFAT; unsupported names fail rather than being rewritten. exFAT holds times from 1980 to 2107: a modification time outside that range, such as the 1969-12-31 that a camera with an unset clock can leave, is shown as the nearest one it can hold, with a warning naming the file. The case-folding table covers ASCII letters only.
  • Previews plugin: classic TIFF only (not BigTIFF), files under 4 GiB. A preview is added, never replaced. A mapped JPEG whose own EXIF cannot be parsed is served unchanged. A metadata DNG’s XMP is served as it is, so its dc:format still says image/dng.
  • One view per config file through the launcher; use separate config files to serve several folders at once.
  • A stable source: files changed while served fail to read; restart after intended changes. A plugin’s prepared state, such as the PMP history snapshot or the previews map, is fixed for the session.
  • Writable views are per session. Written bytes are discarded on stop; only what a plugin saves is kept.
  • NFS mode is experimental.
  • Local use only. There is no TLS, no user authentication and no sharing across a network; the HTTP URL is a localhost capability.

1.14 Troubleshooting

Symptom Cause and fix
Run diskproxy-server. The camera card is not registered; see Registering a new card
A view for NAME is already running. That config’s view is running; use diskproxy status or diskproxy --config FILE stop
Several views are running stop needs --config FILE to choose one
Detach failed. Server left running... An application still has files open; close them and run diskproxy stop again
Mounted volume identity changed. Server left running. The mounted disk is not the one diskproxy attached; check it before doing anything else
Server did not provide a disk URL within 15 minutes. The scan did not finish; the server’s errors are printed above the message
A read fails with an I/O error A source or preview file changed while served; stop and start again
Ratings harvest still running ... The final capture took over two minutes; check the harvester log in the session folder and retry
Ratings check failed; disk left mounted. The replacement walk failed; see the harvester log, fix the cause and retry
Mount point ... is not empty. NFS mode mounts only on an empty folder; empty it or set mountpoint
A DNG shows only a small thumbnail Its map entry is missing, or its preview could not be composed; the server log has a warning

1.14.1 The NFS unmount hang

During early development on macOS 26, unmounting an NFS view hung inside the kernel’s NFS client three times, for between one minute and about half an hour. The volume disappeared at once, but the unmounting process sat in an uninterruptible wait with no NFS traffic, and later NFS mounts queued behind it. Since then the current server has passed 142 consecutive mount/write/unmount cycles without a hang. They were 82 direct cycles, covering both unmount methods, delayed and immediate unmounts and temporary-file-and-rename rewrites, plus 60 cycles through diskproxy start and stop. Unmounts took about 0.1 seconds and the slowest stop took 4.6 seconds. The earlier hangs may have come from the first server version and a kernel client it left degraded; the cause is not proven.

If it happens:

  • leave the stuck process alone; it clears on its own, and killing it does not help;
  • don’t start another NFS view until it clears, because new mounts queue behind it;
  • use a shadow-file view in the meantime; it does not use NFS.

The launcher unmounts with the unmount(2) system call, through diskproxy-server unmount [--force] PATH. Avoid umount and diskutil unmount for NFS views: they wait minutes afterwards for an rpcbind registration this server does not make.

1.15 Development and verification

cargo test --workspace --locked
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings
uv run --python 3.13 python -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_*.py'
uv run --python 3.13 python scripts/check-plugin-example.py

The Rust tests use synthetic sources. They cover path and range validation, read-only access and symlink rejection, exFAT timestamps and checksums, NFC names, composed reads across every piece boundary and change detection on their pieces, the DNG preview patch, JPEG EXIF injection and metadata splicing from a DNG, known preview stamps, map validation, the PMP timezone conventions, ratings capture from JPEG, DNG and sidecar XMP, sidecar naming and journaling, and harvesting by walk and by filesystem events. Integration tests run the server binary for config precedence, unknown settings and HTTP behavior. The Python tests drive the launcher against a mocked server and hdiutil: clean stops, busy detaches, identity mismatches and registration advice. The plugin check registers the hide example in a copy of the repository and serves it.

Beyond the tests, the workflows in this manual were exercised on real data. The PMP plugin resumed an interrupted card at its first new frame, and a new card was registered and ingested with the UTC convention. A previews library of 1.26 million stand-ins served its embedded previews byte for byte, and captured ratings written by Photo Mechanic and exiftool.

Never use real photos, catalogs or application databases as test fixtures.

1.16 Command reference

1.16.1 diskproxy

Command Effect
diskproxy [--config FILE] [start] [SOURCE] [options] Start a view in the background and mount it
diskproxy [--config FILE] status Show each running view’s server and volume, or the selected one
diskproxy [--config FILE] stop Capture pending writes, unmount, stop the server and delete the session; with several views running, --config is required
diskproxy --help Short usage

Options after start are passed to the server, for example --set KEY=VALUE and --label NAME.

1.16.2 diskproxy-server

Command Effect
diskproxy-server Register a camera card with the default PMP config, then exit
diskproxy-server register [options] The same, explicitly
diskproxy-server serve [SOURCE] [options] Serve in the foreground; prints startup JSON
diskproxy-server --config FILE --check Validate and print the startup JSON without serving
diskproxy-server harvest --config FILE --volume PATH [--since EPOCH] [--once] [--interval S] [--stop-file PATH] Capture writes from a mounted writable volume
diskproxy-server unmount [--force] PATH Unmount with unmount(2)
Option Meaning
--config FILE Config file; DISKPROXY_CONFIG sets the default
--plugin NAME, --mode MODE, --label NAME, --port N Override those keys
--set KEY=VALUE Override any key, including plugin settings
--overlay DIR NFS: the overlay folder (the launcher sets it)
--source-offset, --target-offset, --target-zone, --history, --profiles-dir PMP plugin settings
--register PMP: refresh the card’s samples deliberately
